subtype: Child fetches the teacher and a bandage [Actor]
passage: Aadhya, you asked what to do if a friend gets hurt at your sports day. Let me tell you about the Independence Day rehearsal when I was ten. It had rained all night, and the ground was slick red mud. Shankar slipped in the march past and cut his chin on the flagpole stand. Everyone crowded round, shouting. My stomach turned over and I wanted to cry too. But I took one big breath, the way Appa taught me before swimming, and said, "Shankar, stay here, I'm getting Sir." Pradeep, the slowest runner in the class, reached the staff room first! Sir came with the first-aid box, and Shankar got two plasters and a toffee.

qa.q: What did Shankar cut his chin on?
qa.a: The flagpole stand.

qa.q: How was Pradeep feeling when Shankar fell, and what happened to that feeling?
qa.a: Pradeep felt sorry and shaken, stomach turning and close to tears, but one big breath steadied things enough to act.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The moment Pradeep took a breath and chose to run for Sir instead of joining the shouting crowd; that choice brought the first-aid box.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when told "stay here, I'm getting Sir"?
qa.a: Shankar, hurt and surrounded by shouting, probably felt reassured that someone was bringing real help.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling sorry at a friend's fall as a child but staying steady and running to fetch the teacher.

subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
passage:
Since Aditi's Nani died in June, Shalini had taken her calls every night: Aditi crying, going over the hospital days again and again, Shalini listening till one, sometimes two. Pre-boards were three weeks away.
By Raksha Bandhan, Shalini's eyes felt full of sand. She lay awake after the calls, her own chest aching as if it were her Nani. At school she jumped whenever her phone buzzed.
That evening, as she tied a rakhi on her brother's wrist, Aditi's name lit the screen. Shalini looked at it. Her stomach dropped. She turned the phone face down and let it ring out.
"You look exhausted, beta," Mumma said.
"Just exams," Shalini said. The phone buzzed again. She didn't pick it up.

qa.q: Since when had Shalini been taking Aditi's calls every night?
qa.a: Since Aditi's Nani died in June.

qa.q: What is Shalini feeling when Aditi's name lights up the screen?
qa.a: She feels drained and overwhelmed, her stomach dropping, so worn out from carrying Aditi's grief that she lets the call ring out.

qa.q: What could Shalini do instead of avoiding Aditi completely?
qa.a: Tell Aditi honestly she is exhausted and agree a gentler time to talk, tell Mumma the truth instead of "just exams", and encourage Aditi to lean on a trusted adult too.

qa.q: What might it be like for Aditi when the call rings out?
qa.a: Aditi, still grieving, might feel lonely and confused, wondering why the friend who always picked up has gone quiet.

grounding: A teenager absorbs a grieving friend's pain night after night, sleeps badly and starts avoiding her calls.

subtype: Caring role wears the carer down [Actor]
passage:
Subject: Onam in Ward 6

Rehana chechi,
Happy Onam from the medicine ward. There was a pookalam at the nurses' station this morning, and I walked past it without noticing until a patient's daughter pointed it out.
I need to ask you something I can't ask anyone here. In my first month I cried in the washroom after every hard case. The old man in bed 14 who kept asking for his wife. The girl with the burns. I felt all of it. Now, in my third month, I feel almost nothing. Yesterday I snapped at a bystander for asking the same question twice.
Chechi, am I becoming a bad nurse? Did I just stop caring?
Tell me honestly.
Vijay

qa.q: Why did Vijay snap at a bystander?
qa.a: For asking the same question twice.

qa.q: What is Vijay worried about in the email?
qa.a: Vijay feels numb and guilty, worried about becoming a bad nurse who has stopped caring, after feeling every patient's pain so strongly at first.

qa.q: What could Rehana tell Vijay?
qa.a: That the numbness sounds like exhaustion from over-feeling, not a lack of heart, and that talking to a supervisor or counsellor and getting real rest can help the care come back.

qa.q: How might the bystander have felt when Vijay snapped?
qa.a: The bystander, probably already anxious about a relative, likely felt hurt and embarrassed for asking again.

grounding: A nursing student who felt every patient's pain grows numb and irritable and fears having stopped caring.

passage:
I share the flat with Tenzin and Jomon, so I was there when Jomon's phone rang at eleven that night. His father had been taken to hospital in Kottayam. Jomon went grey and started pacing, talking too fast, dropping his charger twice.
Tenzin didn't jump up. I watched Tenzin set down the tea, breathe out slowly, twice, and sit on the arm of the sofa. "Jomon. What would help right now?"
"I don't know. The train, I think. A ticket."
So they did that. Tenzin found a seat on the 5 a.m. train and packed Jomon's bag while Jomon talked to his sister.
At one, I saw Tenzin set an alarm for four and go to bed. "If I'm wrecked tomorrow, I'm no use to him," Tenzin said. I can't say what Tenzin felt, but the flat was calmer for it.

qa.q: At what time did Jomon's phone ring?
qa.a: At eleven that night.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's slow breathing before speaking suggest about Tenzin's state?
qa.a: It suggests Tenzin felt real concern but chose to settle first, staying calm and warm instead of being swept into Jomon's panic.

qa.q: Which of Tenzin's choices would you copy when a friend gets bad news?
qa.a: Settle yourself, ask "What would help right now?", do the practical things like the ticket and the bag, and rest so you can keep helping.

qa.q: What was it like for Jomon to be asked "What would help right now?"
qa.a: Jomon, pacing and panicked, got one clear question to answer, which likely helped him feel less alone and able to act.

grounding: An observer describes a flatmate settling first, asking what would help, and resting so the care can last.

passage:
Tuesday night
Manjula snapped at the new volunteer today, over a misfiled form. Manjula, who once sat with Mrs D'Souza for three hours just holding her hand. After her fourth home visit this week to a family losing someone, she came back and sat in the van with wet eyes, not moving. When I asked, she said, "I'm fine, just tired," and then laughed too hard at nothing.
Afreen, you're her supervisor, I told myself. I should have seen it coming; I kept giving her the hardest cases because she's the best at them.
So: I've moved two of her visits next week to Rohan and me, and she's off on Friday, no arguments. We're having chai tomorrow, just to talk. Caring people need someone caring for them too. That includes me, probably.

qa.q: How many of Manjula's visits were moved next week?
qa.a: Two of her visits, moved to Rohan and Afreen.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling after noticing the changes in Manjula?
qa.a: Afreen feels concerned and a little guilty, having kept giving Manjula the hardest cases because she was the best at them.

qa.q: What steps did Afreen take, and why do they fit?
qa.a: Sharing the load by moving two visits, giving Friday off and setting up a chai talk; together they give Manjula rest, company and less weight to carry.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel about being given Friday off?
qa.a: Manjula might protest at first, but likely feels relieved and cared for, since she has been worn down and tearful.

grounding: A supervisor notices a caregiver growing hard and tearful after hard cases and arranges rest, talk and a shared load.

subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
passage:
Eid morning, and our building's courtyard was full of sheer khurma bowls and new clothes. I live next door to Disha, and I noticed her before anyone else did: arms crossed over her new yellow frock, bottom lip pushed out, kicking the step. Her cousins were getting their eidi, and she had got hers last.
I crouched down. "Your face looks cross, Disha. Are you upset?"
She kicked the step again. Then nodded. "Upset," she said, trying the word.
"Upset because you were last?"
"Yes. Last." She let me hold her hand.
Later I heard her tell her Ammi, "I was upset. Zeenat aunty said."

qa.q: What was Disha wearing?
qa.a: Her new yellow frock.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been thinking when crouching down beside Disha?
qa.a: Zeenat seemed caring and patient, wanting to help Disha find a word for the feeling rather than hurry her out of it.

qa.q: What made Zeenat's question helpful?
qa.a: It named what Disha's face showed, cross, and offered a word, upset, gently, so Disha could try the word without pressure.

qa.q: What was it like for Disha to be offered the word upset?
qa.a: Disha went from kicking the step to nodding and trying the word, and seemed comforted enough to hold Zeenat's hand.

grounding: A neighbour notices a cross child on Eid and gently offers her the word upset to name what she feels.

subtype: Feels something but cannot name it [Actor]
passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, 24 January, Republic Day rehearsal week. Uma
Aditi came to me at the break, clutching the flag she is meant to carry tomorrow. When I asked what was wrong she said, "I feel weird." Weird how? She shrugged, then pressed her hand flat on her stomach. "Here. It's tight. Like a knot." No fever, and she had eaten her tiffin. I asked if it was a sad feeling or a scared feeling or something else. She said, "I don't know," and her eyes filled.
I sat with her on the bench and we breathed together for a while. I will tell her mother at pick-up about the knot and the parade, and on Monday we will try the feelings chart in class.

qa.q: Where did Aditi say the weird feeling was?
qa.a: In her stomach: "Here. It's tight. Like a knot."

qa.q: What might Aditi be feeling but unable to name?
qa.a: Aditi may be nervous or scared about carrying the flag tomorrow, but can only feel it as a tight knot and say "I feel weird".

qa.q: How did the teacher help Aditi look for words without pushing?
qa.a: By offering choices, sad, scared or something else, sitting with her and breathing together, and planning the feelings chart so she can learn names for such knots.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had said "You're fine, go and play"?
qa.a: Aditi would be left alone with a real feeling she could not explain, and might stop trying to describe it next time.

grounding: A child says she feels weird and points to a tight stomach, unable to name the feeling, and a teacher helps her look for words.

passage: Kunal, you keep saying "fine" when your mother asks. Let me tell you about the Losar I turned fifteen, in Dharamshala. Pala had gone to work in Delhi that winter. Everyone kept asking, "Tenzin, what's wrong?" and I always said, "Nothing. Fine." I really believed it. What I did have was headaches, and a stomach that hurt before every meal. Amala took me to the clinic twice; the doctor found nothing. At the Losar feast I sat with my momos going cold, rubbing my forehead. Then my teacher asked a different question: "If that headache could talk, what would it say?" I was quiet a long time. "It would say Pala isn't here." That was the first time I had words for it.

qa.q: How many times did Amala take Tenzin to the clinic?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Tenzin really feeling behind "Nothing. Fine."?
qa.a: Tenzin was missing Pala and sad about the absence, but had no words for it, so the feeling came out as headaches and a sore stomach.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The teacher's question, "If that headache could talk, what would it say?", which gave Tenzin a way to put the ache into words.

qa.q: How might Amala have felt during that winter?
qa.a: Amala was likely worried and puzzled, taking Tenzin to the clinic twice and hearing only "fine" while seeing the headaches.

grounding: An elder recalls answering fine as a teenager while describing aches, until a question helped put the missing into words.

passage:
Looking back on last Eid, I think I got Hemant wrong for a long time. We had been best friends since Class 8 and flatmates for two years, and I told him everything. When my scholarship was cut, I cried in front of him. When his grandfather died in January, he just said, "It's okay, yaar," and went to play cricket. I took it as coldness. I'd ask, "How are you really?" and get "Normal." I felt shut out, as if I was the only one bringing anything to the friendship.
Then at Eid lunch Ammi said, "Rafiq, give him more biryani," and asked him how he was holding up. He stared at his plate and said, "My chest feels heavy since January. I don't know what that is." He wasn't hiding it from me. He just didn't have the words.

qa.q: What did Hemant say when his grandfather died?
qa.a: He just said, "It's okay, yaar," and went to play cricket.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel about Hemant's short answers before Eid?
qa.a: Rafiq felt hurt and shut out, as if the only one bringing anything to the friendship, and took Hemant's "Normal" as coldness.

qa.q: What could Rafiq try now, knowing Hemant struggles to name feelings?
qa.a: Ask about the body or small things, such as "Is your chest still heavy?", and give him time, instead of expecting ready-made feeling words.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hemant to be asked "How are you really?"
qa.a: Hemant may feel stuck and awkward, sensing something heavy but not knowing what to call it, so "Normal" is the only answer he has.

grounding: A young adult feels shut out by a best friend's short answers, then sees it may be difficulty naming feelings, not coldness.

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage:
Every night at ten, after brushing her teeth, Chen opened the notebook by the bed in their Toronto apartment and wrote three lines. Tonight: Tight chest in the 2 p.m. meeting. Word? Maybe dread. Also annoyed when the bus skipped my stop.
On the inside cover was a list she had copied from a feelings wheel: irritated, left out, tender, ashamed, proud. Two months ago, when Nkechi said through tears, "I never know what's going on inside you," Chen had only managed, "Nothing, I think." That had frightened her. The next week she booked a counsellor through work.
Now she read tonight's lines aloud to Nkechi. "Dread," Nkechi repeated softly, and squeezed Chen's hand. "Thank you for telling me."

qa.q: How many lines does Chen write each night?
qa.a: Three lines.

qa.q: Why had Nkechi's words frightened Chen two months ago?
qa.a: Chen felt scared to realise that "Nothing, I think" was all she could say while Nkechi was in tears, and that the missing words were hurting them both.

qa.q: Which of Chen's habits could help someone who struggles to name feelings?
qa.a: Keeping a list of feeling words, noticing body cues like a tight chest, writing a few lines daily, and seeing a counsellor when it strains love or work, as Chen did.

qa.q: How does Nkechi seem to feel when Chen reads the lines aloud?
qa.a: Nkechi seems moved and grateful, repeating "Dread" softly and thanking Chen for sharing.

grounding: An adult learns feeling words through a list, body cues, nightly notes and counselling after a partner feels shut out.
